newsitem.title: USA: Glendale says court denies two govt. motions.
newsitem.headline: Glendale says court denies two govt. motions.

text.p: Glendale Federal Banks said on Thursday the chief judge of the U.S. Court of Federal Claims denied a government motion, ruling that the company may present evidence in support of the alternative measures of expectation damages, reliance damages and restitution for the government's alleged breach of contract.
Judge Loren Smith also denied the government's motion to exclude evidence of lost profits or to impose a limit on the amount of Glendale's expectation damages, the company said.

The trial in Glendale's lawsuit against the federal government is scheduled to begin on Feb. 24, 1997. Its purpose is to determine the amount of damages the government owes Glendale, the company said.
In a July 1, 1996, decision, the U.S. Supreme Court found the government liable for breaching a contract with the bank, according to Glendale.

Glendale's lawsuit stems from a 1981 contract with the government in which the bank took on a $783 million potential liability by merging with a failing Florida thrift. In exchange, the government promised Glendale Federal that it could include the goodwill created by the merger as capital, to be amortized over 40 years. In 1989, the government said the the remaining goodwill must be eliminated in five years.
Glendale Federal, which said it has sought unsuccessfully to initiate settlement talks with the government, said the judge urged the parties to consider settling the dispute out of court.
